paragraphs: Baker, here's the big idea. Elihu gets one thing exactly right, and he says it twice so nobody misses it: "Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act unjustly" (Job 34:10), and "God does not act wickedly, and the Almighty does not pervert justice" (Job 34:12). God made everything and holds every breath (Job 34:14-15). He is not partial to the rich over the poor, because "they are all the work of His hands" (Job 34:19). And "There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide" (Job 34:22). That is solid ground, friend, and you can stand on it.

Now here's the catch, and I think it's the lesson hiding under the lesson. Elihu takes that true thing and swings it at Job. He says Job speaks "without knowledge" (Job 34:35), and he wants Job tried to the utmost. But Job has said he is without transgression (Job 34:6), and Elihu is quoting Job back to him like a prosecutor. I think Elihu is so busy defending God that he forgets to listen to the man who's hurting. A true statement about God can still be used in an unkind way, and I've held a hot tray the wrong way myself.

So what do you do with it, baker? Hold on to the truth that God is just, even on the days when you can't see what He's doing. Elihu says it himself: "when He remains silent, who can condemn Him?" (Job 34:29). Then be slow to hand that truth to a hurting friend like a verdict. Some words are good for the bakery and some words need a gentler touch, and wisdom knows the difference. This story is far from finished, so keep your ears open.
